study.title: Isaiah 27 - Judgment on enemies, beware of the vineyard, and restoration of the people
study.overview: Isaiah 27 presents a sequence of announcements of judgment and mercy. The chapter begins with the defeat of the Leviathan, an image of powers hostile to God, and soon passes into the figure of the vineyard, which represents the people of the LORD. God not only protects this vineyard, but also disciplines his people with measure, in order to lead them to repentance and the purification of idolatry. The chapter ends with the hope of the meeting of the scattered by means of a great trumpet, so that they may return to worship on the holy mountain in Jerusalem.

outline.title: Judgment against the enemy and care of the vineyard
outline.explanation: The chapter opens with the defeat of a symbolic enemy and then with the song of the fruitful vineyard. God watches, waterers and protects his people, but also calls peace with him, showing that his discipline is not arbitrary, but a restorer.

outline.title: Future fruit and purification of sin
outline.explanation: Israel is depicted as a people who will take root, blossom and fill the land with fruit. At the same time, the discipline of the LORD is described as moderate, aiming to remove guilt and eliminate idolatrous altars, so that sin may be truly forgiven.

outline.title: Desolation of the city and final meeting of the scattered
outline.explanation: The fortified city becomes deserted, showing the fall of what seemed safe. Then comes the agricultural image of the selective gathering of the people, and at last the great trumpet gathers the scattered of Assyria and Egypt to worship the LORD in Jerusalem.

study.context: The notes provided link the chapter to God's action for his people and against his enemies. Matthew Henry mentions Jerusalem's liberation from Assyrian danger as a close setting, but also says that the text is generally expressed for church encouragement at other times. Notes do not require a unique historical identification for each symbol; instead, they treat the images as spiritual and prophetic representations of God's action throughout history.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that God governs both judgment and restoration. The Leviathan may symbolize evil or oppressive powers that rise up against the Lord, but his defeat is assured. At the same time, God's people are compared to a vineyard that he himself keeps continually, showing persevering and paternal care. Divine discipline does not contradict her grace; it serves it, for it seeks to produce repentance, remove idolatry and restore fellowship. The hope of a broad restoration also appears: Israel will flourish, the scattered will be gathered together and the worship of the Lord will be reestablished. In evangelical reading, this can be seen as pointing to the full fulfillment of redemption in Christ and to the final meeting of God's people.

scholarViews.insight: The death of Leviathan symbolizes the end of evil, the demonic forces and all that opposes God.
The chapter shows that God takes care of his vineyard, that is, his people, as a vigilant and gracious owner.
The great trumpet is understood as an image of the gathering of the scattered, linked to the final meeting of the people of God.

questions: In what ways does this chapter call me to trust that God defeats powers that I can't win alone?
In what areas does my life show that I need not only protection but also repentance and peace with God?
How does the hope of the meeting of the scattered correct a small and local view of God's work?
study.practice: Take this passage to prayer with three movements: worship for God's victory over evil, personal examination of idolatries that need to be removed, and active hope of belonging to the people he collects and makes fruitful. In practice, this can mean abandoning false dependencies, seeking reconciliation with God and others, and persevering in fidelity even in times of dispersion or fragility.
study.uncertainty: Interpretative notes differ in some symbolic details, especially about Leviathan and the great trumpet. There are also limits to accurately identify the historical background of each image, because the notes provided treat the chapter in a more theological and prophetic way than chronologically. It is not safe to go beyond what the text and notes support.
